html:
At eight in the evening on 8 November 2016 the prime minister, Narendra Modi, said on television that the 500 and 1,000 rupee notes would stop being legal money at midnight. They made up 86 per cent of the cash in India.

The stated aims were to wipe out untaxed "black" money held in cash, to make forged notes useless, and to cut off money for terrorism. Only a handful of people had known. Old notes could be paid into a bank until the end of the year; new 500 and 2,000 rupee notes would replace them.

There were not enough new notes. For weeks people queued for hours at banks and cash machines, which had to be refitted for notes of a new size. Limits on withdrawals changed again and again. Farmers could not buy seed, day labourers went unpaid, and small firms that worked in cash shut down. A number of deaths in the queues were reported.

In 2018 the Reserve Bank said that 99.3 per cent of the old notes had come back. Almost no black money had been destroyed; it had been paid in. Growth slowed for several quarters.

Payments by phone grew fast (see UPI), and more people filed tax returns. Modi's party won the next big state election easily. The Supreme Court upheld the measure in 2023.
sum: At eight in the evening on 8 November 2016 the prime minister, Narendra Modi, said on television that the 500 and 1,000 rupee notes would stop being legal money at midnight. They made up 86 per cent of the cash in India.
